candidates.label: Caesarea (coastal ruins south of Haifa)
candidates.support: The site preserves extensive Herodian and Roman-period harbor and city remains, built over the earlier Hellenistic settlement of Strato's Tower; it is uncontested as the location of Caesarea Maritima.

summary.text: Caesarea Maritima was a Mediterranean port that Herod the Great built from the ground up over about twelve years, on a stretch of coast between Joppa and Dora that had no good natural harbors. Herod named the city for the Roman emperor Augustus, building it in white stone with palaces, public buildings, a theatre, and an amphitheatre. Its showpiece was an artificial harbor that the Jewish historian Josephus compares in size to the Piraeus at Athens, built by sinking huge stone blocks into twenty fathoms of water to form a mole 200 feet wide; a temple holding statues of Rome and of Caesar stood on a rise overlooking the harbor, visible to approaching ships from far out at sea.

history.text: By Paul's day, Caesarea was the residence of the Roman governor of Judea. Acts describes it as the home of Cornelius, a centurion of the "Italian Regiment," whose Gentile household was baptized at Peter's command, and as the place where Paul was held "in Herod's palace" and kept in custody for two years under the governors Felix and Festus, until his final voyage to Rome.

Riots between the city's Gentile and Jewish populations helped touch off the Jewish revolt against Rome. During that war, Roman soldiers at Caesarea hailed the general Vespasian as emperor, and his son Titus later celebrated his brother Domitian's birthday there by having 2,500 Jewish captives fight wild animals in the city's amphitheatre.

Caesarea was finally destroyed in 1265, during the Crusades. Today visitors to the site can see the ruins of a cathedral built where Herod's temple had stood, and of two aqueducts that brought water to the city.

scripture.textWEB: But Philip was found at Azotus. Passing through, he preached the Good News to all the cities until he came to Caesarea.
When the brothers knew it, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
Now there was a certain man in Caesarea, Cornelius by name, a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment,
On the next day they entered into Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends.
Behold, immediately three men stood before the house where I was, having been sent from Caesarea to me.
When Herod had sought for him and didn’t find him, he examined the guards, then commanded that they should be put to death. He went down from Judea to Caesarea, and stayed there.
When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the assembly, and went down to Antioch.
On the next day, we who were Paul’s companions departed and came to Caesarea. We entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us, bringing one Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we would stay.

He called to himself two of the centurions, and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred men armed with spears, at the third hour of the night.”
But on the next day they left the horsemen to go with him, and returned to the barracks.
When they came to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.
“I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive.” He commanded that he be kept in Herod’s palace.
After five days, the high priest, Ananias, came down with certain elders and an orator, one Tertullus. They informed the governor against Paul.
Festus therefore, having come into the province, after three days went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea.
However Festus answered that Paul should be kept in custody at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to depart shortly.
When he had stayed among them more than ten days, he went down to Caesarea, and on the next day he sat on the judgment seat, and commanded Paul to be brought.
Now when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus.

Festus said, “King Agrippa, and all men who are here present with us, you see this man about whom all the multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both at Jerusalem and here, crying that he ought not to live any longer.
They of the circumcision who believed were amazed, as many as came with Peter, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was also poured out on the Gentiles.
He commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay some days.
But when two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus, and desiring to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in bonds.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch."

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod Agrippa I (ruler: Herod Agrippa I)
Roman province of Judea (ruler: Procurators, e.g. Antonius Felix, Porcius Festus)
Roman province of Judea (ruler: Legates, with a legion now based at Jerusalem)
politicalHistory.note: An administrative upgrade (a legate instead of a procurator), not a border or name change.
